narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Heap, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 6 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Two values that are the wrong way round cannot both be where they are. Exchanging them puts both right in a single move.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n log k) in the worst case, O(k) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Dynamic Programming, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 11 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Write it down in one place, and read it from there rather than working it out again.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(amount × coins) in the worst case, O(amount) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

debrief.summary: You worked the sunken vault corridor one lantern at a time until the obsidian vault resolved. What this problem is built to teach: The fewest coins for each amount reuses smaller answers: try every coin, take one plus the best for the remainder, and keep the minimum. The run is bounded by O(amount × coins) time and O(amount) extra space, and that bound comes from the algorithm rather than from how carefully you played.
